summary: This document describes the current requirements and requests for enhancements to the format of the canonical version of RFCs. It defines terms to clarify which stages of document production are being discussed. The requirements will guide later format changes. It updates RFC 2223.

eli5.summary: This is a wish list for how RFC documents should look and be built, so future changes follow clear goals.

questions: what is the canonical format of an rfc
what are the rfc format requirements
what rules did rfc 2223 set for rfc pages
subtitle: A 2013 wish list for how RFCs should look: which plain-text rules to keep, add and retire.

tldr.problem: The RFC format had been plain ASCII text with fixed page and line limits for decades. Authors and readers asked for diagrams, wider characters, reflowable text and metadata, but no proposal had clear consensus.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines terms for the stages of document production, summarizes the arguments for and against each requested change, and then lists 16 numbered requirements: some kept, some added, and a few retired.
tldr.outcome: It sets requirements only. The detailed rules were left to a future RFC and the RFC Style Guide. It is Informational and updates RFC 2223.

today: RFC 6949 is an Informational document that updates RFC 2223, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements only; the detailed rules were to be written in a future RFC and the RFC Style Guide.

sections.title: Why the RFC Format Was Reviewed
sections.content:
The RFC Series began as a collection of memos, some handwritten, some typed, some produced on mainframes. As the tools changed, the people behind the Series chose US-ASCII and, after a period of variability, a well-defined presentation format. That format has proved persistent and reliable across many devices, operating systems and editing tools, and the RFC calls its stability a continuing strength.

Newer technology, such as small devices and advances in display technology, has produced a growing desire to adapt the format. Suggestions had been made since the format stabilized, but none had developed clear consensus. This document, from the IAB with the RFC Series Editor and the Independent Submissions Editor as authors, captures the requirements. Its focus is the canonical format of RFCs.
sections.eli5: RFCs have always looked like plain typed pages, and that has worked well. Now people read on phones and tablets, so they want to know whether the look should change.

sections.title: Stages of a Document and Their Formats
sections.content:
The RFC defines terms so that a format discussion says which stage it means. The canonical format is the authorized, recognized, accepted and archived version of the document. The publication format is what readers see or print after publication. The revisable format is what the RFC Editor uses to produce publication formats. The submission format is what authors send to the RFC Editor.

It also defines reflowable text (text that wraps as the window or font size changes) and metadata (information that describes structure or elements such as topic or author). The RFC notes that the RFC Editor already calls things such as the stream, status (Updates, Obsoletes), category and ISSN metadata.
sections.eli5: Think of a recipe: the version you send in, the version the editors work on, the official copy kept forever, and the copy you print. This RFC gives each of them a name.

sections.title: The Existing Format Rules
sections.content:
The rules come from RFC 2223 and a draft revision. Characters are ASCII. Each page is limited to 58 lines followed by a form feed, and each line to 72 characters. Overstriking and underlining are not allowed, there is no hyphenation at the right margin, and footnotes are not used. Text is single spaced within a paragraph, with one blank line between paragraphs.

RFC 2223 allowed other formats such as PostScript, but the ASCII text version is the primary one and any other version must match it. The RFC advises cross-references by section number rather than page number, because pagination changes when a document is reformatted.
sections.eli5: The old rules were like a strict school worksheet: same page size, same line length, only plain letters, no fancy extras.

sections.title: Arguments For and Against Each Change
sections.content:
The RFC lists the main concerns and gives both sides of each, without treating them as requirements. ASCII art: simple diagrams force clear prose and are more accessible, but state diagrams, flows with several parties and equations would be clearer as real graphics. Character encoding: ASCII is easy to search and to retype or rescan, while UTF-8 would allow author names and examples in their own scripts. Pagination: pages ease reference and printing; removing them helps reading on more devices and pushes authors toward subsections.

Reflowable text reads better on mobile screens but may hurt graphics and tables. Metadata could make reading more efficient but adds process overhead and a backward-compatibility burden.

The RFC also weighs RFC-specific tools and a markup language (XML or HTML) as the revisable format. The RFC Editor wanted a more efficient process: of the RFCs published in 2012, approximately 65% were submitted with an XML file, yet each RFC still had an nroff file made at the end, which cost time and lost data from the XML.
sections.eli5: Some people like the plain old style because it works everywhere. Others want pictures and more letters so ideas are easier to show. The RFC writes down both sides fairly.

sections.title: The 16 Format Requirements
sections.content:
Four original requirements are retained: published content must not change whatever the format; the canonical format must stay persistent and reliable across devices and platforms; at least one publication format must be plain text; and boilerplate and structure follow the current RFC and Style Guide rules.

Eight requirements are added for the Series (numbers 5 to 12). They include accessibility for people with visual disabilities (alternative text for images, limited use of color), English as the official language with ASCII required for text needed to understand or implement the technology, and extensible metadata tags. Graphics may be ASCII art or a more complex form to be defined, such as SVG line art, and color and grayscale are not accepted. The canonical format must render into self-contained publication formats, ASCII art and code need fixed-width, non-reflowable text, at least one publication format must print well on standard paper, and the structure should let programs identify code such as MIB modules and ABNF.

Four more cover the RFC Editor's process (13 to 16): replace the final conversion to nroff with an accepted revisable format, work with the minimal number of files per submission, limit the number of publication formats, and require tools that check layout and format details.

Three old rules are to be retired: pagination, the maximum line length, and the limit to 100% ASCII text. Detailed rules were left to a future RFC. The security section says the document does not concern interactions between Internet hosts, so it has no specific security considerations.
sections.eli5: The RFC ends with a checklist: keep the rules that protect old documents, add rules so everyone can read them, and drop the rules about page length and line length.
